items.prompt: As this unit defines it, what is "choosing battles"?
choices: Deciding, deliberately and case by case, whether a disagreement is worth spending real political capital on, using a consistent method
Avoiding conflict whenever possible to preserve relationships
Fighting every disagreement you have a strong opinion about
Letting your manager decide which disagreements are worth raising
items.explanation: Choosing battles isn't avoidance and it isn't fighting everything — it's a deliberate, case-by-case call made with a consistent method rather than mood, habit, or conflict-avoidance.
items.reference:
⚖️ Not "avoid everything"
⚖️ Not "fight everything"
🎯 A deliberate, consistent method, applied case by case

Why: Both extremes — fighting everything and fighting nothing — are named directly in L1 as unsustainable; the real skill is the method that tells the two kinds of situation apart.

items.prompt: Someone says "I just go with my gut on which disagreements to push" and calls this choosing battles. Does that match the unit's definition?
choices: No — the unit's version is a deliberate, consistent method, not instinct or mood
Yes — gut feeling is exactly what the unit recommends
Yes, as long as the gut feeling is usually right
No — the unit says you should never trust your own judgment at all
items.explanation: The unit explicitly contrasts "how strongly you feel in the moment" with a real method, because both genuine principles and mere annoyance can produce equally strong feelings — instinct alone is a bad predictor.
items.reference:
⚖️ Not "avoid everything"
⚖️ Not "fight everything"
🎯 A deliberate, consistent method, applied case by case

Why: Both extremes — fighting everything and fighting nothing — are named directly in L1 as unsustainable; the real skill is the method that tells the two kinds of situation apart.

items.prompt: According to L1, what happens if you fight every battle?
choices: You burn out and people stop taking your objections seriously, including the ones that matter
You quickly become the most respected person in the org
Nothing changes — objecting to everything has no real cost
You automatically win every important argument
items.explanation: Fighting everything burns you out and, just as importantly, teaches people to discount your objections across the board — including the rare ones that are genuinely worth their attention.
items.reference:
🔥 Fight everything → burnout + objections ignored
🫥 Fight nothing → principles erode
🎯 Neither extreme is sustainable

Why: L1 names both failure modes directly and frames the whole unit as the deliberate method for telling them apart.

items.prompt: According to L1, what happens if you fight none of your battles, ever?
choices: A long enough string of "not worth it this time" adds up to no longer having anything you'll reliably stand on
You become more effective, since you never spend social capital
It has no long-term effect on how you see yourself
You automatically become better liked by everyone
items.explanation: The unit is explicit: never fighting erodes your own principles and self-respect over time, even though any single instance of yielding looks harmless in isolation.
items.reference:
🔥 Fight everything → burnout + objections ignored
🫥 Fight nothing → principles erode
🎯 Neither extreme is sustainable

Why: L1 names both failure modes directly and frames the whole unit as the deliberate method for telling them apart.

items.prompt: As L1 defines it, what is "identity drift"?
choices: The gradual process where someone who learned political skill for real goals starts, in small defensible steps, using it for its own sake
A single dramatic decision to start playing politics for personal gain
Any use of political skill at all, regardless of intent
Losing an argument you were right about
items.explanation: Identity drift is defined specifically by being gradual and cumulative — a series of individually defensible small steps, not one dramatic betrayal.
items.reference:
🪞 Not one dramatic decision
🐢 Many small, individually defensible steps
👻 No single moment marks the crossing

Why: L1's four small compromises (M4, M8, M11, M14) each looked reasonable alone — the pattern only shows up laid out together, which is exactly the mechanism identity drift describes.

items.prompt: Why does L1 say identity drift is harder to catch than a single obvious betrayal?
choices: Because each individual step is defensible on its own, so no single moment triggers an alarm
Because it always happens instantly, with no warning at all
Because it only affects people who are already dishonest
Because it's caused entirely by other people's actions, not your own choices
items.explanation: The danger is precisely that no individual step looks like a betrayal — the pattern is only visible from a distance, laying multiple small choices side by side, which is hard to do from inside the process.
items.reference:
🪞 Not one dramatic decision
🐢 Many small, individually defensible steps
👻 No single moment marks the crossing

Why: L1's four small compromises (M4, M8, M11, M14) each looked reasonable alone — the pattern only shows up laid out together, which is exactly the mechanism identity drift describes.

items.prompt: L1 says the real question isn't "was any one of the four compromises wrong." What is the real question it poses instead?

Whether the engineer should quit immediately

items.explanation: L1 deliberately reframes away from judging any single item and toward the harder problem: losing the ability to tell, from the inside, where the line between reasonable trade-off and real compromise sits.

items.prompt: Why does L1 emphasize that each of the four compromises, alone, still looks like a reasonable trade-off?

items.explanation: The point isn't that any one item was catastrophic — it's that each one clearing a low, individually reasonable bar is precisely the mechanism that lets a real pattern accumulate unnoticed.

items.prompt: L1's key terms distinguish a "principle" from a "preference." Which best captures the difference?
choices: A principle is a line that, if crossed, changes something true about who you are or what you'll tolerate; a preference is just how you'd rather things go
A principle is anything you feel strongly about in the moment; a preference is anything you don't care about
There is no real difference — both terms mean the same thing
A principle is whatever your manager says matters; a preference is whatever you personally think matters
items.explanation: The distinction is about what crossing the line actually changes — a principle changes something true about you if crossed, a preference is just a matter of taste about how things go.

items.prompt: L1 says confusing a principle with a preference "in either direction" causes problems. What does "either direction" mean here?
choices: Treating a preference as sacred is a problem, and so is treating a real principle as negotiable
It only means treating preferences as sacred — treating principles as negotiable is always fine
It refers to whether you're arguing with a superior or a subordinate
It means the definitions of principle and preference change depending on who you're talking to
items.explanation: Both errors are named: over-elevating a mere preference into something sacred, and under-weighting a genuine principle into something negotiable — either mistake makes battle-choosing go wrong.

items.prompt: As L1 defines it, what does "institutional toxicity" mean?
choices: A pattern where the organization's political environment itself, not a specific person or incident, is fundamentally incompatible with someone's values
Any single unpleasant interaction with a difficult coworker
A company that has too many meetings
A person who is deliberately malicious toward everyone around them
items.explanation: Institutional toxicity is specifically about the environment itself, not any one incident or person — the case where individual skill, applied from inside, doesn't actually fix the underlying problem.

items.prompt: As L1 defines "reversibility," which of these is more reversible?
choices: A bad decision that can be revisited next quarter
A precedent that, once set, is very hard to undo
Both are equally reversible
Neither is reversible in any meaningful sense
items.explanation: L1 contrasts a bad decision that can be revisited later against something that forecloses permanently, like a precedent or a person's trust — reversibility is exactly this axis.

items.prompt: What are L2's three questions, in order, for deciding whether a battle is worth having?
choices: Principle or preference? What's the actual cost of losing? Is it reversible?
Who is more senior? Who is more likeable? Who will win anyway?
How angry am I right now? Will I regret staying silent? Is this embarrassing?
Is this technical or interpersonal? Is it public or private? Is it urgent?
items.explanation: The three questions, asked in order, are: is this a principle or just preference/ego, what is the concrete downstream cost of losing, and is the outcome reversible or does it foreclose something permanently.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Principle or preference?
2️⃣ What's the actual cost of losing?
3️⃣ Is it reversible?

Why: A battle worth having scores high on all three; a battle not worth having scores low on at least two — the order matters because principle is checked before cost or reversibility even come into play.

items.prompt: Someone proposes deciding whether to fight a battle using only "how strongly do I feel about this right now." What does L2 say is wrong with that approach?
choices: Both real principles and mere annoyance can produce equally strong feelings, so intensity alone is a bad predictor
Nothing — feelings are always an accurate signal of what's actually a principle
Feelings should be ignored completely and never factored in at all
It's fine as long as you feel strongly enough, regardless of the topic
items.explanation: L2 opens by ruling out gut feeling specifically because strong feelings don't reliably distinguish a real principle from mere ego or preference — that's exactly why the three-question method exists.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Principle or preference?
2️⃣ What's the actual cost of losing?
3️⃣ Is it reversible?

Why: A battle worth having scores high on all three; a battle not worth having scores low on at least two — the order matters because principle is checked before cost or reversibility even come into play.

items.prompt: In L2's worked table, both disagreements look identical from the outside ("a colleague disagrees with your approach in a design review"). What actually determines which one is worth fighting?

How the disagreement is phrased in the meeting
Whether the disagreement happens in a public channel or a private one
items.explanation: The table's whole point is that surface shape doesn't tell you anything — one case hides a real, user-facing correctness issue, the other is a fully reversible style preference. Only checking what's actually at stake reveals which is which.

Why: Both look identical on the surface ("disagreement in a design review") — only checking what's actually at stake, not how the argument is dressed up, tells them apart.

Why: Each step individually looks harmless — that's the mechanism, not a flaw in it, which is exactly why it's hard to catch from inside.

items.prompt: L2 says the honest test for drift isn't "did I make one bad call." What is it instead?
choices: Periodically listing the actual small choices from the last few months and seeing what they add up to, not the principles you'd state if asked
Asking your manager to grade your recent political choices
Waiting for a single dramatic event that makes the answer obvious
Comparing yourself to the most political person you know
items.explanation: The test is recurring and concrete: list actual recent choices, not stated principles, and check for a gap between the two — a gap is the signal, not any single item.

items.prompt: Why does L2 say "I can justify each individual choice" isn't a sufficient defense against drift?
choices: Because local justification is exactly what someone mid-drift would also say — the problem only shows up looking at the pattern across time
Because justifications are always dishonest by definition
Because only a manager's judgment counts, never your own
Because it's actually a completely sufficient defense and no further check is needed
items.explanation: Each step in a slow drift is, by construction, individually justifiable — that's the mechanism, not a flaw in it. "I can justify each one" is necessary but not sufficient.

items.prompt: Which of these is one of L2's three questions for telling "the incident is the problem" apart from "the organization is the problem"?
choices: Would a different, equally principled person in your seat face the same pressure?
Has this ever happened to a competitor company?
Would a therapist agree this is stressful?
Is this the first bad thing that's ever happened to you at work?
items.explanation: That's the first of the three checklist questions — if the compromise seems tied to the org's structural incentives rather than your own choices, that's a signal it's institutional.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Would a different, equally principled person face the same pressure?
2️⃣ Has raising it, ever, changed anything?
3️⃣ Is "winning" even a coherent goal here?

Why: None of these produce a clean yes/no alone — it's a genuinely hard judgment call, and getting it wrong in either direction (leaving too early, staying too long) has a real cost.

items.prompt: L2's checklist asks "is winning even a coherent goal here." What is this question actually probing?

items.explanation: In a genuinely toxic environment, "I'll fix it from inside" can quietly stop being a real plan and become a justification for staying — this question forces scrutiny of whether there's an actual plausible path to change.

items.prompt: A teammate's change follows documented team conventions but uses a style you personally find ugly, with no measurable effect on correctness or maintainability. Using the three-question method, what's the verdict?

items.prompt: What real cost does L2's Checkpoint attach to fighting low-stakes battles like a code-style disagreement repeatedly?

items.explanation: The named cost is credibility erosion: repeatedly fighting low-stakes disagreements is the mechanism by which people learn to discount your objections, even the ones that genuinely matter.
